blocks.text: 1. Transposed Convolution

blocks.alt: A small feature map goes through learnable upsampling, forming transposed convolution

blocks.text: Global Average Pooling, the previous topic, collapsed feature maps down to single values. Transposed Convolution is a technique for genuinely increasing spatial resolution rather than reducing it, a genuinely new direction explored throughout this topic.
It is sometimes called the reverse of the ordinary Convolution Operation already covered, though the precise nature of that reversal gets clarified carefully throughout this topic.
2. A New Direction After A Module Of Shrinking

blocks.alt: Regular convolution shrinks while transposed convolution grows

blocks.text: This connects back to the Convolution Operation, Pooling, and Stride, all already covered. Every technique covered so far in this module genuinely shrinks or preserves spatial size, never increases it.
Transposed Convolution instead genuinely grows spatial size, a fundamentally new direction that this topic introduces for the very first time in this module.
3. Why Growing Size Is Genuinely Needed
A genuinely important motivating problem connects forward to tasks needing genuinely pixel-level output, like Object Detection and Computer Vision Tasks, covered later in this course.

These tasks genuinely need output the same size as the original input, not a genuinely shrunk feature map, a real, practical requirement that every technique covered earlier in this module cannot satisfy on its own.
4. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: A small input has learned weights spread it out into a larger output

blocks.text: Transposed Convolution's genuinely core idea inserts genuinely empty space between existing values, then applies an ordinary convolution, already covered in its own topic, to that expanded, spaced-out input.
This produces a genuinely larger output than the original input, rather than a smaller one, achieving the exact opposite effect from the shrinkage already covered throughout most of this module.

blocks.text: 5. Not An Exact Inverse

blocks.alt: Transposed convolution is not a true mathematical inverse

blocks.text: This connects back to the ordinary Convolution Operation, already covered. A genuinely important, precise clarification: Transposed Convolution does not exactly reverse a convolution's own lost information.

It genuinely reverses the shape transformation, but the exact original values are genuinely not recoverable, since the ordinary convolution's own weighted-sum computation, already covered, is not perfectly invertible.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: This clarification, already covered in this topic, is genuinely important to avoid a common misconception. Transposed Convolution produces a larger output shape, but it is genuinely not the mathematically exact inverse operation of a convolution.

blocks.text: 6. Learnable Upsampling

blocks.alt: Fixed upsampling is compared against transposed convolution, which learns the upsampling

blocks.text: This connects back to filters, already covered as genuinely learned weights in Filters and Kernels. Transposed Convolution's own filter weights are genuinely learned through training too, exactly like an ordinary convolution's filters.

This happens unlike simpler, fixed upsampling methods that merely genuinely duplicate or interpolate values, giving Transposed Convolution the genuine flexibility to learn exactly how to upsample most usefully for a given task.
7. A Known Practical Issue: Checkerboard Artifacts

blocks.alt: Transposed convolution can produce checkerboard pattern artifacts

blocks.text: A genuinely real, known practical issue connects back to uneven filter overlap during the upsampling process, already covered in this topic. This uneven overlap can genuinely produce a visible checkerboard pattern artifact in the output.

This is a genuinely well-documented, real practical concern that practitioners must carefully manage when using Transposed Convolution, often through careful choices about filter size and stride, already covered in its own topic.
8. Stride, Reversed

This connects back to Stride, already covered in its own topic. A genuinely larger stride in Transposed Convolution produces genuinely more upsampling, the reverse relationship from ordinary convolution.

This holds where a genuinely larger stride instead produced a genuinely smaller output, already covered there, exactly the reversed direction that gives this entire technique its own genuinely apt name.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Transposed Convolution Is Genuinely Necessary

blocks.alt: Needing to upsample an image points toward using transposed convolution

blocks.text: This connects forward to Semantic Segmentation, a Computer Vision Task covered later in this course. It genuinely needs pixel-level output the same size as the input, already covered in this topic.

This connects forward to Generative Models, covered later in this course, needing to genuinely produce full images. Transposed Convolution, already covered, is a genuinely common building block there too.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simplified Transposed Convolution, inserting empty space between values before applying a small filter, illustrating the core idea already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

small_input = np.array([
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4],
])  # already covered as the genuinely small input in this topic

stride = 2  # already covered as stride, reversed in this topic

# Insert empty space between existing values, already covered as the core idea in this topic
expanded_size = small_input.shape[0] + (small_input.shape[0] - 1) * (stride - 1)
expanded = np.zeros((expanded_size, expanded_size))
expanded[::stride, ::stride] = small_input

print("Original small input:\n", small_input)
print("\nExpanded, with empty space inserted (already covered as the core idea in this topic):\n", expanded)
print(f"\nOriginal shape: {small_input.shape}, expanded shape: {expanded.shape}, genuinely larger, already covered as this topic's own core purpose")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the small 2x2 input expanded into a genuinely larger, sparser grid with values inserted at spaced-out positions, illustrating the first step already covered as this topic's own core idea before an ordinary convolution would then be applied.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Transposed Convolution genuinely increases spatial resolution rather than reducing it.
It is the first technique in this module to genuinely grow spatial size instead of shrinking it.
Tasks needing pixel-level output, like Semantic Segmentation, genuinely require this kind of upsampling.
It works by inserting empty space between values, then applying an ordinary convolution.
It reverses the shape transformation of a convolution, but does not recover the exact original values.
Its filter weights are genuinely learned through training, unlike simpler, fixed upsampling methods.
Uneven filter overlap during upsampling can produce a visible checkerboard pattern artifact.
A larger stride here produces more upsampling, the reverse relationship from ordinary convolution.
Next up: Depthwise Convolution, a technique for genuinely reducing computation by processing each channel independently.
